messages.subject: panel.grid theme inheritance
messages.body_plain:
I've been busy, so I've been a bit behind with all the new changes recently, so I could just be missing something here.

I was exploring the new theme system (which is pretty darn cool, btw) and discovered this (in R 2.15.1, ggplot2 9.2.1):

dat <- data.frame(x = 1:5,y = 1:5)
p <- ggplot(dat,aes(x = x,y = y)) + geom_point()

#No change
p + theme(panel.grid = element_line(colour = "red"))

# Only changes panel.grid.major?
p + theme(panel.grid = element_line(size = 2))

I was sort of under the impression that changes to panel.grid ought to propagate down to panel.grid.major and minor (and then .x and .y). Am I missing something about how the inheritance mechanism works?

messages.subject: Re: panel.grid theme inheritance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joran -

You're probably right that it should (conceptually) inherit the color. The issue is that for theme_grey(), the colors and sizes of the lines are set for these items:
* panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "white"),
* panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey95", size = 0.25),

It probably would make sense to define panel.grid and then have the .major and .minor inherit properties from that. Sizes could be relative, with rel(), but I'm not sure how to deal with the different colors.

FYI, you can inspect inherited element properties with calc_element().

calc_element('panel.grid.major.x', theme_grey(), verbose = TRUE)
# panel.grid.major.x --> panel.grid.major
# panel.grid.major --> panel.grid
# panel.grid --> line
# line --> nothing (top level)
# List of 4
#  $ colour  : chr "white"
#  $ size    : num 0.5
#  $ linetype: num 1
#  $ lineend : chr "butt"
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_line"

mytheme <- theme_grey() + theme(panel.grid = element_line(colour = "red"))
calc_element('panel.grid.major.x', mytheme, verbose = TRUE)
# panel.grid.major.x --> panel.grid.major
# panel.grid.major --> panel.grid
# panel.grid --> line
# line --> nothing (top level)
# List of 4
#  $ colour  : chr "white"
#  $ size    : num 0.5
#  $ linetype: num 1
#  $ lineend : chr "butt"
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_line"

And if you just want to see the properties without inheritance, you can run theme_grey() and have it print out the entire theme, or select a particular element:

theme_grey()$panel.grid.major
# List of 4
#  $ colour  : chr "white"
#  $ size    : NULL
#  $ linetype: NULL
#  $ lineend : NULL
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_line"

-Winston

messages.subject: new approach to custom grid grobs
messages.subject_clean: new approach to custom grid grobs
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have committed to r-devel some experimental changes to how grid grobs can be customised (essentially an alternative set of hook methods, makeContext() and makeContent(), to use instead of preDrawDetails() and drawDetails()).

There is a document describing the motivation for the change and various examples of usage at http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/R/customGridRedesign.pdf

The document includes an example of how 'gtable' classes could be reimplemented with this new design, plus a small discussion of the resulting benefits (see pages 26-29 of the document)

I have done some testing to check that things still work and I think the changes are worth it, but any further testing and feedback would be extremely welcome.

Paul

> I have committed to r-devel some experimental changes to how grid grobs can
> be customised (essentially an alternative set of hook methods, makeContext()
> and makeContent(), to use instead of preDrawDetails() and drawDetails()).
>
> There is a document describing the motivation for the change and various
> examples of usage at
> http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/R/customGridRedesign.pdf
>
> The document includes an example of how 'gtable' classes could be
> reimplemented with this new design, plus a small discussion of the resulting
> benefits (see pages 26-29 of the document)
>
> I have done some testing to check that things still work and I think the
> changes are worth it, but any further testing and feedback would be
> extremely welcome.
>
> Paul

Sure! At the moment, the vtest package is only on github:
  https://github.com/wch/vtest
 You can install it with
  install_github('vtest', 'wch')

There's information about it here:
  https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system

Here's an example of a result set generated by vtest:
  http://stdout.org/~winston/vtest-gtable/html/
And here's a diff set generated by vtest, comparing results from two different git commits:
  http://stdout.org/~winston/vtest-gtable/diff/

That reminds me - it expects your project to have a git repository, and it won't work without one.

The examples above were tests of ggplot2. But you probably will want to use it with grid graphics The gtable tests are a better example to start from:
  https://github.com/hadley/gtable/tree/master/visual_test
The output looks like this:
  http://stdout.org/~winston/gtable-vtest-demo/html/

Good luck!
-Winston

As plyr and ggplot2 become more widely used, the development process
is getting more conservative.  Part of this is avoiding features that
appeared in the latest version of R (which is a pain if you're in an
environment that can only upgrade yearly).  I haven't started doing
any formal testing, but it's on my long-term horizon.
